question: A farmer presents with excessive salivation, lacrimation, urination, defaecation, emesis, miosis, and muscle fasciculations. Which toxidrome does this represent, and what is the first-line antidote?

answers.text: Cholinergic toxidrome (SLUDGE + BBB); first-line antidote is atropine

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. SLUDGE (Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, GI cramps, Emesis) plus Bradycardia, Bronchospasm, Bronchorrhoea (BBB) = cholinergic toxidrome from organophosphate poisoning. Atropine is the first-line antidote, titrated to dry secretions.
Incorrect. Anticholinergic toxidrome presents with dry skin, mydriasis, tachycardia, and urinary retention — the opposite of what is described. This case describes excess cholinergic activity.

Partially correct on the toxidrome, but pralidoxime is the second-line agent used to reactivate acetylcholinesterase before aging; atropine is the FIRST-line antidote to control secretions and bronchoconstriction.
Incorrect. Opioid toxidrome presents with miosis, respiratory depression, and loss of consciousness — without the salivation, lacrimation, defaecation, and fasciculations described here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the Classification and Toxidrome Recognition blocks. The SLUDGE+BBB mnemonic defines organophosphate poisoning. Atropine controls muscarinic effects first; pralidoxime reactivates AChE (before aging is complete).
Good. Toxidrome recognition is time-critical — atropine must be given immediately in large doses (2–4 mg IV, then doubled every 5–10 minutes to dry secretions) before pralidoxime.
